parts: Lesson 11: Adolescence and Its Challenges — Summary

Adolescence is the period of transition from childhood to adulthood, when the person changes physically and psychologically and new social roles are demanded; the child moves from dependency to autonomy. In the Indian social system it falls under Brahmacharya (apprenticeship), the first ashram. Erikson held that each life stage has a specific crisis; adolescents must integrate various roles into a consistent self-identity or they experience confusion over who they are.

Adolescence is a stage of stress, strain and storm with many ambiguities; uncertainty about one's role causes conflicts. Delinquency, suicides and drug and alcohol addiction may begin; career is planned and philosophies of life are moulded.

Adolescence is both. It begins with biological changes: the pre-adolescent growth spurt occurs in girls mostly at 9–12 years and in boys at 11–14 years, followed by secondary sexual characteristics: girls – rounding of hips, breast development, pubic hair, menstruation; boys – pubic hair, facial hair, change of voice. Its length is mainly social (when one leaves home, gets a job, can vote). Adolescents in western and eastern societies behave differently because of social norms, expectations and family structure.
Factors determining the pattern of transition

Speed of transition (very fast change, little preparation); length of transition (early maturers are expected to act like adults; prolonged adolescence fosters dependence); discontinuities in training (trained to be dependent and submissive, now asked to take responsibility); degree of dependency (depends on childhood training; parents foster dependency); ambiguous status (in India the child follows parents' footsteps, in open societies each chooses own course); conflicting demands of parents, teachers, peers and community; degree of realism (looks like an adult but may not feel ready); motivation (insecurity lowers motivation; removing barriers raises it).

Developmental tasks are the problems individuals typically face at different periods of life. Havighurst listed ten for adolescents: new and more mature relations with age mates of both sexes; a masculine or feminine social role; accepting one's physique and using the body effectively; emotional independence of parents and other adults; assurance of economic independence; selecting and preparing for an occupation; preparing for marriage and family life; developing intellectual skills and concepts necessary for civic competence; desiring and achieving socially responsible behaviour; acquiring a set of values and an ethical system. Success brings success with later tasks; failure brings unhappiness and difficulty. In advanced cultures a person becomes an adult at the legal age; in simple cultures young people show adult status through puberty rites.

Pubescence is the beginning of adolescence. Growth spurt: girls about 10–11, boys 12–13 years, linked to the pituitary gland (controls adrenals, gonads, thyroid); rapid growth lasts 3–4 years, peak at average 12.6 years for girls and 14.8 for boys; a child may grow 6–8 inches and gain 18–22 kg in a year. Asynchronization: skeletal and muscular growth is faster than learning to use the new muscles; the lower face lags behind the upper; legs grow faster than the stem; hands and feet grow first. Sex hormones: testosterone in males, estrogen in females, secreted by the gonads. Sequence in girls: breast enlargement, pubic hair, menarche, axillary hair; in boys: testes enlargement, pubic hair, axillary hair, voice change, beard. Primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs (menarche in girls, first ejaculation in boys); secondary are observable such as voice change and hair. Boys' strength rises with androgens, broader shoulders, bigger chest and lungs; girls' strength rises slowly because of biology and because culture encourages them to be weak and dependent. Average is not necessarily optimal.

Gender relates to a society's beliefs about traits and behaviours of males and females; gender roles are expectations about the roles and behaviour of each. Gender identity (knowing one is a boy or girl) is established by age 3–4; gender consistency (one remains the same sex despite changes in clothing or behaviour) is acquired at 6–7 years.
